system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2141-02-18 22:59:00 to 2141-02-23 18:36:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with productive cough, high fever, confusion, and leukocytosis. Imaging revealed lung opacities suggestive of pneumonia or aspiration, and a urine culture confirmed E. coli UTI, likely complicated by a malpositioned Foley catheter. His delirium was attributed to the infection and recent cocaine use. He was treated with IV antibiotics, transitioned to oral Augmentin, and improved clinically. His chronic kidney disease remained stable, and he was discharged home with follow-up plans for urology, infectious disease, and primary care. Blood cultures were negative at discharge but required outpatient follow-up.
problems: Pneumonitis due to inhalation of food or vomitus
Delirium due to conditions classified elsewhere
Infection and inflammatory reaction due to indwelling urinary catheter
Epilepsy, unspecified, without mention of intractable epilepsy
Escherichia coli [E. coli] infection in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site
Streptococcus infection in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site, streptococcus, group D [Enterococcus]
Urinary catheterization as the cause of abnormal reaction of patient, or of later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of procedure
Late effects of motor vehicle accident

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  The patient is a ___ male with altered mental status. 
Evaluate for intracranial hemorrhage or stroke.

EXAMINATION:  Non-contrast head CT.

COMPARISONS:  ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Contiguous axial images were obtained through the brain.  No
intravenous contrast was administered.

FINDINGS:  There is no evidence of hemorrhage, edema, mass effect, or acute
territorial infarction.  The gray-white matter differentiation is preserved. 
The ventricles and sulci are normal in size and configuration. The paranasal
sinuses and mastoid air cells are well aerated.  There is no acute fracture.

IMPRESSION:  No acute intracranial process.

AP PORTABLE CHEST, ___ AT 20:52 HOURS.

HISTORY:  Altered mental status and intubation.

COMPARISON:  Multiple priors, the most recent dated ___.

FINDINGS:  Consistent with the given history, an endotracheal tube is
identified with the distal tip approximately 6 cm from the carina.  A
nasogastric tube is also identified with the sidehole projecting over the
gastroesophageal junction.  As previously noted, posterior spinal
stabilization rods are again evident and incompletely imaged in chest field of
view.  Also compared similar to prior, there are markedly diminished lung
volumes with elevation of bilateral hemidiaphragms.  No focal consolidation or
superimposed edema is noted.  The mediastinum is otherwise unremarkable.  The
cardiac silhouette is within normal limits for size accounting for patient and
technical factors.  No effusion or pneumothorax is noted.

IMPRESSION:  Grossly no evidence of aspiration although limited study due to
low lung volumes.  Endotracheal tube in satisfactory position.  Consider
advancing NG tube 5 cm for optimal placement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. ___ . You're in the hospital because you were found with confusion and trouble breathing. We had to put a breathing tube in to help you. Do you remember what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I... don’t really remember. My mom said I passed out after dinner?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. Your mom called EMS. You were very drowsy, with pinpoint pupils and slow breathing. We gave you Narcan, but it didn’t help much, so we intubated you for safety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t mean to... I just took my usual meds. I’ve been feeling down lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your toxicology screen showed benzodiazepines, opiates, and cocaine. You’re prescribed oxycodone and clonazepam, but the test suggests other substances were involved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I might’ve taken something extra... I was stressed. But no cocaine. I haven’t done that in months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t confirm the source, but the combination likely caused your altered mental status. Your heart rate was very slow, and your blood pressure was high—common with mixed drug effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my heart okay? I’ve had issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EKG showed bradycardia, but no heart damage. Cardiology doesn’t think you need a pacemaker. Your rate improved after we lowered your blood pressure with hydralazine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. What about my kidneys? They’ve been bad for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine was 2.9 on admission—consistent with your baseline CKD. We’re adjusting your meds for kidney safety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had UTIs before that made me confused. Could this be another one?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great point. Your urine showed nitrites and leukocytes, so we started IV antibiotics just in case. But the culture came back with no growth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly not, but because you have a chronic Foley and past UTIs, we’re finishing a short course of oral nitrofurantoin to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about my back pain and seizures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your Keppra for seizures. Your osteomyelitis and back pain are stable. No new pressure sores.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’m really sorry about all this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Psychiatry saw you and thinks this wasn’t a suicide attempt—more of a mistake. They’ve referred you for counseling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re off the ventilator now. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. My head’s clearer. Was I really on a breathing machine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just for one day. Your oxygen levels were good, and you started following commands, so we extubated you yesterday afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. Any more tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a head CT—it was normal, no bleeding or stroke. Chest X-ray showed no pneumonia or aspiration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My mom said my blood pressure’s been high at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 160s. We treated it as a hypertensive emergency because of your altered mental status. You’re back on amlodipine, but at a lower dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why lower it? I was just started on 7.5 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because of the overdose risk. We’re starting you on 2.5 mg daily and will adjust with your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs look good. White count is down, kidney function stable. We’re almost done with IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can stop the IV meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll switch to two more days of oral nitrofurantoin. It’s safe for your kidneys and you’re allergic to other options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any other changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re simplifying your pain meds. You’ll be on 20 mg sustained-release oxycodone every 8 hours, plus 5 mg as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s less than before. Will it be enough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re reducing to lower overdose risk. If pain isn’t controlled, your PCP can adjust. We’ve also added alprazolam for anxiety as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ve been really anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Last urine test was clear. No signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly by tomorrow. We want to make sure you’re stable and have follow-up arranged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need help at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Social work is setting that up. You’ll go home with your mom, and home health will assist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow. Your vitals are stable, labs are good, and you’re alert.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take the nitrofurantoin twice daily for two more days. Keep all your meds as listed. And please follow up with your PCP, urologist, and psychiatrist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I want to get better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Avoid any unprescribed drugs. If you feel overwhelmed, call your counselor or go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Here’s your discharge summary and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ve learned a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if anything changes.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with altered mental status and respiratory failure following a drug overdose involving benzodiazepines, opiates, and cocaine. He was intubated for airway protection and managed in the ICU with supportive care, including IV hydralazine for hypertension and antibiotics for suspected UTI. Toxicology and psychiatry consultations indicated a non-suicidal mixed ingestion. He was successfully extubated on hospital day two, completed a course of antibiotics, and stabilized medically. His chronic conditions, including CKD, neurogenic bladder, and seizure disorder, were managed without complication. He was discharged home with simplified medications, a short course of oral nitrofurantoin, and referrals for psychiatry, substance use counseling, and primary care follow-up.
